source.title: RAIGen: Rare Attribute Identification in Text-to-Image Generative Models
source.authors: S. V. Sreelatha; Dan Wang; S. Belongie; Muhammad Awais; Anjan Dutta

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different method and model family, but reports how decomposition tools and architecture relate to the interpretability of selected latent features. This bears on V4, not on the Qwen neuron-pole audit or the language-model explanation tests.
record.gate_note: Rows record reported interpretability results for selected diffusion-model features relevant to V4. The toy experiment on activation frequency, generated-image attribute-presence scores, and amplification results do not measure V4's interpretability claim and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses Matryoshka SAEs as a tool to find rare attributes in diffusion models. Its interpretability numbers are fractions of the top-10 SAE latents chosen by its own ranking, used to tune and validate RAIGen (ranking ablation, sample budget, prompt robustness). It never measures what share of a model's own neurons are interpretable, nor how that share changes with tools or architecture. So it does not test V4 or any other version; the reader's T2/V4 link is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that RAIGen, combining MSAEs with a frequency × distinctiveness Minority Score, finds interpretable rare attributes that diffusion models encode but rarely express. They report that it works across SD v1.4, v2.1 and XL and extends to FLUX, supports cross-model auditing, and enables amplification through prompt revision. The record's emphasis on FLUX producing weaker candidates is a side observation, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Matryoshka sparse autoencoders and image-level semantic evaluation in text-to-image diffusion models, rather than auditing language-model neuron poles or testing written explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies with decomposition method (vanilla SAE versus MSAE), ranking criterion, number of generated samples, and diffusion architecture/hook point.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla-SAE latents in SD fragment concepts (separate left-eye and right-eye units), while MSAE coarse latents are described as more coherent. The evidence is qualitative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The decomposition tool (vanilla vs Matryoshka SAE) changes how coherent the learned features in diffusion models are.

fits_no_version.finding: In FLUX.1-schnell, a transformer diffusion model, more high-scoring SAE latents are weakly interpretable than in U-Net models. The authors attribute this partly to architecture and hook point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The interpretability of SAE features depends on the diffusion architecture and on the hook point chosen.

fits_no_version.finding: Among the 10 least-frequent SAE latents, 62.5% were judged uninterpretable. The share of interpretable selected latents also rises with the number of training samples (0.1 to 0.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SAEs trained on generative models, rarely firing and under-trained latents are often uninterpretable.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The interpretability rates concern selected features, not all neurons. Interpretability is judged from annotations and qualitative checks rather than a ground-truth inventory of features; the authors note that coverage and precision are difficult to quantify without ground-truth minority-attribute annotations. The FLUX.1-schnell comparison is qualitative and uses a selected hook point.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported metrics, including attribute presence, amplification, likelihood, alignment, and the activation-frequency toy experiment, do not measure V4 interpretability and were left out. No claim-version-specific results were omitted.

untested.parts: All: neuron shares in language models across sizes and architectures.
All: InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons and recursive generalization.
The share of a model's own neurons that are interpretable, and how it changes with tools or architecture. Only SAE latents chosen by the method's ranking are assessed.
All: whether explanations from activating examples predict firing.
All: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

missing.what: Low-scoring (majority) SAE latents are described as diffuse and fragmented across many units. These are SAE features, not neurons, so the finding matches no version.

record.verdict_notes: All interpretability numbers are from GPT-5.2 annotations of top-ranked SAE latents. The authors also report that MSAE coarse-level size and sparsity affect fragmentation.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole shares and testing explanations on held-out activations.
Language-model neuron-pole shares across dense and mixture-of-experts models or parameter scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization.

The study examines selected sparse-autoencoder features in diffusion models, not the share of all original model neurons that are interpretable; it does not test InceptionV1-sized vision models or the essay's 5% to 99% estimates.
Attribution graphs, circuit explanations, and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated scoring of language-model neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: SD v1.4
rows.operation_detail: Compared vanilla SAE features with MSAE features for minority-attribute discovery.
rows.measure: Qualitative semantic coherence and fragmentation of selected features
rows.baseline: MSAE comparison described in Appendix G.7
rows.value: The SAE surfaced some attributes, but features were considerably more fragmented; examples included separate neurons responding to the right and left eye.
rows.note: The authors say fragmentation could make neurons appear to represent minorities while capturing only partial or redundant features.
rows.check: Qualitative look at vanilla-SAE latents in a method ablation (G.7). These are SAE features, not model neurons, and no share is given. Belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: SD v1.4
rows.operation_detail: Used MSAE features for minority-attribute discovery and compared their coherence with vanilla SAE features.
rows.measure: Qualitative semantic coherence and fragmentation of selected features
rows.baseline: Vanilla SAE comparison described in Appendix G.7
rows.value: The authors report that hierarchical control over granularity mitigates fragmentation and yields more faithful, interpretable discovery of underrepresented attributes.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; no whole-network interpretability share is reported.
rows.check: The authors' own method (MSAE) compared with an alternative, described qualitatively. SAE latents, not model neurons.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Selected top 10 neurons by activation-frequency-only ranking and assessed annotation interpretability.
rows.measure: Fraction of selected neurons judged interpretable
rows.baseline: Other ranking strategies compared in Table 8
rows.note: The authors describe low-frequency neurons as sometimes noisy or uninterpretable.
rows.check: Selection value: fraction of top-10 latents picked by a ranking ablation (Table 8) that the annotator judged interpretable. This is method performance, not a neuron-interpretability share.

rows.subject: FLUX.1-schnell
rows.operation_detail: Assessed interpretability of high-scoring features at the selected transformer hook point.
rows.value: The authors report a higher fraction of high-scoring but weakly interpretable neurons than in U-Net-based models; several candidates had diffuse or non-localized heatmaps.
rows.note: The authors suggest that the hook point and few-step sampling may contribute, and call for more systematic hook-point selection.
rows.check: Qualitative remark that FLUX shows more weakly interpretable high-scoring SAE latents than the U-Net models, at one hook point. SAE latents, not model neurons, and no number is given. Belongs in fits_no_version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected RAIGen features in SDXL under the reported prompts and settings
reader_labels.reason: Selected-feature interpretability reaches 0.70–1.00 across the additional prompts, and the paper qualitatively reports that MSAE mitigates the fragmentation seen with vanilla SAE features (R2, R6–R14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Alternative feature-selection settings, limited sample budgets, and the tested FLUX.1-schnell hook point
reader_labels.reason: Interpretability varies with selection and sample count, and FLUX.1-schnell has a higher fraction of weakly interpretable candidates than the U-Net-based models; the measurements cover selected features rather than the share of all model neurons (R1, R3–R5, R15–R19).
